A history lesson · Land of Israel, 167–37 BCE

The Hasmonean Period

From Mattathias at Modi’in to Herod’s siege of Jerusalem: the Maccabean revolt, the priest-kings of an independent Judea, and the scholarly debate over the Torah’s place in their world

Prepared by Scholar · October 2026

This lesson follows the Hasmoneans, the priestly family that began as rebels against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV in 167 BCE, ruled an independent Judea for most of a century, and lost it to a civil war, to Rome and to Herod in 37 BCE. It covers the revolt, the rededication of the Temple that Hanukkah commemorates, the family’s rise from rebels to priest-kings, their conquests, and the world of Pharisees, Sadducees and the Dead Sea Scrolls in which they ruled.

The main sources, 1 and 2 Maccabees and Josephus, were written by people with views, and the lesson says who claims what. Section 10 sets out one recent scholarly argument, by Yonatan Adler, about when Torah observance became widespread in Judea, with the main responses to it. Items that could not be checked against a source other than Wikipedia are marked [unconfirmed]. The maps are schematic and the images are free files from Wikimedia Commons.

1The lesson

From Modi’in to Jerusalem, 167–37 BCE

Eleven sections · about 70–90 minutes · 3 maps, a family tree, a reign chart, 14 images

1. The Seleucids and Antiochus IV’s decrees, c. 200–167 BCE

Key dates
  1. c. 200Seleucids take Judea from the Ptolemies
  2. 175Jason buys the high priesthood
  3. 169Antiochus IV plunders the Temple
  4. 168Rome orders him out of Egypt
  5. Dec 167Decrees; altar to Zeus in the Temple

After Alexander the Great died in 323 BCE, his generals divided his empire. For about a century Judea, a small temple-state around Jerusalem, belonged to the Ptolemies of Egypt. Around 200 BCE the Seleucid king Antiochus III beat the Ptolemaic army at Panion, near the sources of the Jordan, and took the whole region. The scholarly dating of the battle is 200 or 198 BCE. Josephus preserves a letter in which Antiochus III grants Jerusalem tax relief, money for Temple repairs and the right to live by its “ancestral laws” (Antiquities 12.138–144). Its authenticity has been debated.

The Seleucids soon needed money. Rome defeated Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BCE, and the Treaty of Apamea (188 BCE) imposed a very large indemnity. In Jerusalem, the high priest was the head of the community and, under imperial rule, the king’s man in the city. That made the office worth buying. According to 2 Maccabees 4, Jason, brother of the high priest Onias III, offered the new king Antiochus IV (175–164 BCE) money for the post and for permission to found a gymnasium and to enrol “Antiochenes in Jerusalem.” A gymnasium was a Greek school and sports ground. First Maccabees 1:11–15 says that some Jews wanted to “make a covenant with the nations” and built one. Soon Menelaus outbid Jason for the high priesthood (2 Macc 4:23–26). The sources disagree about who Menelaus was. Second Maccabees 3:4 and 4:23 imply that he was not of the old high-priestly family, while Josephus (Ant. 12.238–239) says he was Onias’s brother.

In 169 BCE Antiochus IV invaded Egypt. On his way back he entered the Temple and carried off its gold vessels and treasures (1 Macc 1:20–24; 2 Macc 5:11–21). In 168 BCE he invaded again, and at Eleusis near Alexandria the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas drew a circle around him in the sand and told him to answer the Senate before he stepped out of it. He withdrew (Polybius 29.27; Livy 45.12). The humiliation fell, directly or indirectly, on Jerusalem. Both books report an attack on the city and the building of a Seleucid fortress, the Akra, overlooking the Temple (1 Macc 1:29–40; 2 Macc 5:24–26). Its exact site in Jerusalem is still debated.

In 167 BCE the king’s decrees followed. First Maccabees 1:41–64 and 2 Maccabees 6:1–11 describe them in similar terms. Burnt offerings, sacrifices and libations in the Temple were forbidden. Sabbaths and festivals were not to be kept. Circumcision was forbidden, and parents who circumcised their sons were punished. Copies of the law were to be torn up and burned. Altars to other gods were to be built, and pigs and other unclean animals were to be sacrificed. On 15 Chislev in the Seleucid year 145 (December 167 BCE) “an abomination of desolation” was built on the altar, and ten days later the first sacrifice was offered on it (1 Macc 1:54, 59). The phrase is also used in the book of Daniel (11:31, 12:11), whose visions most scholars date to this crisis. Second Maccabees 6–7 adds the stories of the martyrs, among them the old scribe Eleazar and the seven brothers and their mother.

Why did the king do it? This is one of the great questions in ancient Jewish history. The Jewish sources blame Antiochus himself and “lawless” Jews. The German-Jewish historian Elias Bickerman (Der Gott der Makkabäer, 1937) argued that the decrees were not a pagan attack on Judaism but the work of Hellenizing Jewish reformers, Menelaus above all, who wanted to modernize their religion and persuaded the king to impose it. Victor Tcherikover (Hellenistic Civilization and the Jews, 1959) saw a social conflict between a rich Hellenizing urban elite and rural traditionalists. Erich Gruen (“Hellenism and Persecution,” 1993) rejects these explanations, including the financial one, and treats the persecution as a display of royal power after the humiliation in Egypt. All three views have critics. The evidence is one-sided because we have only the Jewish accounts, and both books were written by people who needed the king to be wicked.

Why it matters

The decrees did something no earlier empire had done to the Jews. They attacked the Temple cult and the practices that marked Jews as Jews, in the Temple and in the villages. That made resistance a religious duty and not only a matter of tax or politics. The Hasmonean state grew out of this conflict, and the Hasmoneans’ later claim to rule rested on having defended the law.

2. Mattathias and the revolt at Modi’in, 167–166 BCE

Key dates
  1. 167Mattathias kills the king’s officer at Modi’in
  2. 167–166Guerrilla war; Hasideans join
  3. 166/5Mattathias dies; Judah takes command

The revolt began in a village. First Maccabees 2:1–5 introduces Mattathias, son of John, a priest of the family (“course”) of Joarib, who had left Jerusalem and lived in Modein with five sons: John called Gaddi, Simon called Thassi, Judas called Maccabeus, Eleazar called Avaran and Jonathan called Apphus. Josephus calls their ancestor Asamonaios, the origin of the name “Hasmonean” (Ant. 12.265). The nickname “Maccabee” is usually explained as “hammer” from Aramaic, but that is a guess.

The king’s officers came to Modein to enforce the sacrifices (1 Macc 2:15–28). Mattathias refused to take part. When another Jew stepped forward to sacrifice, Mattathias killed him on the altar, killed the king’s officer, tore down the altar and cried, “Let everyone who is zealous for the law and supports the covenant come out after me.” He and his sons fled into the hills. First Maccabees reports that the “Hasideans,” a group “devoted to the law,” then joined them (2:42).

Where was Modein? The sources place it in the hills west of Jerusalem, on the way to the coastal plain. Josephus says it was a village in Judea (Ant. 12.265). The modern city of Modi’in, founded in the 1990s, took its name from the tradition, but the ancient site is not certain [unconfirmed]. Several ruins nearby have been proposed, among them the village of al-Midya. The “Tombs of the Maccabees” at Horbat ha-Gardi are generally regarded as a later construction. First Maccabees 13:25–30 says that Simon built a great monument at Modein for his parents and brothers.

The first reported turning point was a tragedy. A thousand Jews who had fled to the desert were attacked on the Sabbath and let themselves be killed rather than fight (1 Macc 2:29–38). Mattathias and his followers then decided that they would fight in self-defence on the Sabbath (2:39–41). Josephus tells it the same way (Ant. 12.272–277). The decision is often cited as an early precedent for the later rabbinic principle that saving a life overrides the Sabbath. Mattathias’s band attacked altars and enforced circumcision in the villages. He died in the Seleucid year 146 (166/165 BCE), and his deathbed speech (1 Macc 2:49–70) names Judah the military leader and Simon the adviser.

A note on sources. First Maccabees was probably written in Hebrew and survives in Greek. Its last chapter looks back on the reign of John Hyrcanus I, so it was composed late in the second century BCE or soon after. It is a family history of the Hasmoneans and says that God gave deliverance “through the hands” of this house (5:62). Second Maccabees, which survives in Greek, is an abridgement by an unknown author of a five-volume work by Jason of Cyrene (2 Macc 2:23). It does not mention Mattathias at all. It begins with Judah, stresses the Temple and the martyrs, and does not present the Hasmoneans as a dynasty. Josephus later retold both. For the Hasmonean period after 104 BCE, there is no Maccabean narrative at all and we depend on Josephus, who in turn relied on lost sources, above all the court historian Nicolaus of Damascus, and who also quotes the geographer Strabo (and Strabo’s source Timagenes).

Why it matters

Mattathias’s act at Modein turned a defence of the Temple into a war led by a priestly family from the countryside. Because First Maccabees was written for that family, the Hasmonean story is told from the winners’ side. When you read “the Maccabees” in a source, ask who wrote it and for whom.

3. Judah Maccabee and the rededication, 166–160 BCE

Key dates
  1. 166–165Victories at Beth-horon and Emmaus
  2. 164Beth-zur; Temple retaken
  3. 25 Chislev, Dec 164Altar rededicated
  4. 162Defeat at Beth-zechariah; peace; Alcimus
  5. 161/0Nicanor killed at Adasa; Rome treaty
  6. 160Judah falls at Elasa

Judah (Judas Maccabeus) turned the band into an army. First Maccabees 3–4 tells of three victories over Seleucid forces, all won in the hill country where an army from the plain had to climb. At Beth-horon, on the ascent from the coastal plain, he beat the commander Seron (3:13–24). At Emmaus, in the western foothills, he beat a force under Gorgias and Nicanor (4:1–25). Then in 164 BCE he beat the regent Lysias at Beth-zur, south of Bethlehem (4:26–35). Bezalel Bar-Kochva’s Judas Maccabaeus (1989) is the standard military analysis. First Maccabees gives very large figures for the enemy, which are not reliable. Second Maccabees (8:1–36; 10–11) tells the same story with a different order of events.

After Beth-zur, Judah went up to Jerusalem. The Seleucid garrison still held the Akra, so he posted men to keep it quiet while priests “without blemish” cleaned the Temple (1 Macc 4:41–43). The old altar had been defiled. They pulled it down, stored the stones “until a prophet should come to tell what to do with them” (4:44–46), and built a new altar of uncut stones, with new vessels, a new lamp stand and a new table. On 25 Chislev in the Seleucid year 148, exactly three years after the first pagan sacrifice, they offered the first sacrifice on it. They celebrated for eight days and decreed that the dedication (Greek enkainia, Hebrew ḥanukkah) should be kept every year (4:52–59). Second Maccabees 10:1–8 describes the same events. It says the festival was kept for eight days “in the manner of the Festival of Booths,” and that they had been in the mountains and caves during the previous Booths. It adds that they lit the lamps and put out the bread of the Presence (10:3). Josephus calls the festival “Lights” (Ant. 12.316–325).

The rededication did not end the war. Judah attacked Seleucid allies in Idumea, Ammon, Gilead and the coast (1 Macc 5), and Simon went to Galilee (5:21–23). Antiochus IV died on campaign in the east in 164 or 163 BCE, and the two books order this event differently [unconfirmed]. His son Antiochus V, still a child, came with the regent Lysias in 162 BCE. They besieged Beth-zur and the Temple, defeated Judah at Beth-zechariah, where Judah’s brother Eleazar was killed trying to stab an elephant (1 Macc 6:28–47), and made peace. The Seleucid government gave back the right to follow ancestral laws (6:55–60; compare the letters at 2 Macc 11:16–38, whose dates and authenticity are debated).

Then politics changed. In 162 BCE Demetrius I seized the throne and made Alcimus, who was of Aaron’s line but not of the Hasmonean family, high priest. The Hasideans accepted him as a legitimate priest (1 Macc 7:12–14). A Seleucid general, Bacchides, killed sixty of them, according to 1 Maccabees (7:16). Judah killed Nicanor at Adasa on 13 Adar (7:43–49), in March of 161 or 160 BCE depending on which Seleucid calendar 1 Maccabees follows, an anniversary the Jews kept for some time (“Nicanor Day,” 2 Macc 15:36). Around this time he sent envoys to Rome (1 Macc 8; see section 9). In 160 BCE Judah met Bacchides at Elasa with far fewer men and fell. His brothers Jonathan and Simon buried him at Modein (9:1–19).

Why it matters

Judah’s Temple was the only part of the story that every later tradition remembered. Everything Judah achieved was military and religious: he did not found a state or a dynasty. When he died in 160 BCE, the Seleucid government still controlled Jerusalem’s citadel, appointed its high priest, and could have ended the movement.

4. Jonathan and Simon: from rebels to rulers, 160–134 BCE

Key dates
  1. 160Jonathan leads the rebels
  2. Autumn 152Jonathan made high priest by Alexander Balas
  3. 143Jonathan seized and killed by Tryphon
  4. 142“Yoke of the nations” removed; Simon’s first year
  5. 141Akra surrendered
  6. 18 Elul 140Great assembly confirms Simon
  7. 134Simon murdered at Dok

After Elasa, the rebels chose Jonathan as leader (1 Macc 9:28–31). For some years he was a guerrilla chief in the Judean desert, and Bacchides fortified towns around Jerusalem and Judea, including Beth-zur and Gazara (9:50–52). A peace followed around 157 BCE, and Jonathan lived at Michmash and “judged the people” (9:73). Jonathan’s opportunity came from Seleucid weakness. In 152 BCE Demetrius I and a rival, Alexander Balas, competed for his support. Demetrius gave him permission to raise an army. Balas wrote offering him the high priesthood, a purple robe and a golden crown. Jonathan accepted Balas’s offer, and on the Feast of Booths in the Seleucid year 160 (autumn 152 BCE) he put on the sacred vestments (10:15–21). A man from a non-Zadokite priestly family was now high priest. Josephus’s version (Ant. 13.35–46) agrees. Qumran writers later denounced a “Wicked Priest” (see section 9).

For ten years Jonathan changed sides skilfully in the Seleucid succession wars, and each king paid him. Demetrius II, in 145 BCE, transferred three districts, Aphairema, Lydda and Ramathaim, to Judea (1 Macc 11:34), and Jonathan took more of the coast. He renewed the Roman friendship and, according to 1 Maccabees 12, wrote to Sparta. In 143 BCE the Seleucid general Tryphon invited Jonathan to Ptolemais, seized him, and later killed him at Baskama (1 Macc 12:39–48; 13:23). He was buried at Modein (13:25).

Simon, the last of the five brothers, led Judea from 143 BCE. He fortified Adida, took Joppa, which gave Judea a port (1 Macc 12:33; 13:11; 14:5), took Beth-zur and Gazara (Gezer), and in the spring of 141 BCE the Akra surrendered after a long siege (13:43–52). He cleansed it and moved in. Meanwhile Demetrius II, pressed by the Parthians and by Tryphon, granted Judea exemption from tribute. First Maccabees 13:41–42 says that in the Seleucid year 170 (142 BCE) “the yoke of the nations was removed from Israel,” and the people began to date documents “in the first year of Simon, the great high priest, commander and leader of the Jews.” Many modern historians treat 142 BCE as the start of Jewish independence. This was independence in a limited sense. Judea did not become a state recognized by treaty. It was a client of whoever held Antioch, and a Seleucid king could still send an army, as Antiochus VII soon showed.

On 18 Elul in the Seleucid year 172 (September 140 BCE) a great assembly of priests, people and elders voted Simon high priest, commander and “ethnarch” of the Jews, and the office was to be hereditary “until a trustworthy prophet should arise” (14:25–49). The decree was engraved on bronze tablets and set up on Mount Zion. It was Simon’s family who now held priesthood, command and rule together, and the “prophet” clause admitted that the arrangement was provisional. Antiochus VII at first gave Simon the right to mint coins (15:6), but then withdrew all concessions and sent an army. Simon’s sons John and Judah fought it off (15:25–16:10). In the eleventh month of the Seleucid year 177 (February 134 BCE), Simon’s son-in-law Ptolemy, governor of Jericho, murdered Simon and two of his sons at a banquet in the fortress of Dok, hoping to take power (16:11–16). A third son, John, escaped.

Why it matters

The Hasmoneans became rulers step by step and by accepting titles from Seleucid claimants. The decree of 140 BCE gave them legitimacy from their own people, but they were not of the family of Zadok, which had held the high priesthood, or of David. Every later quarrel about the Hasmoneans, the Pharisees’ and Qumran’s complaints in particular, starts from this gap.

5. John Hyrcanus I: expansion and conversion, 134–104 BCE

Key dates
  1. 134Hyrcanus succeeds; Antiochus VII besieges Jerusalem
  2. 129Antiochus VII dies in Parthia
  3. c. 112–108Idumea; Mount Gerizim temple destroyed
  4. c. 108–107Samaria taken and razed
  5. 104Hyrcanus dies; Aristobulus I rules

John (Yohanan) Hyrcanus, the surviving son of Simon, was high priest and ruler for about thirty years (Josephus gives thirty-one). He escaped the murder at Dok, took Jerusalem, and, according to Josephus, held out against Ptolemy until a sabbatical year forced the siege to be lifted (Ant. 13.228–235). The first test came from Antiochus VII Sidetes, the most energetic Seleucid king for a generation. In 134/133 BCE he besieged Jerusalem and, after a long siege, made terms. Hyrcanus gave hostages, paid tribute, and had part of the walls pulled down. Josephus says he also took three thousand talents from the tomb of David to buy the king off (Ant. 13.236–249). Antiochus VII declined the advice of some of his counsellors, reported by Diodorus (34/35.1), to destroy the Jews’ city and customs. Hyrcanus joined the Parthian campaign, in which Antiochus VII was killed in 129 BCE (13.250–253). After that, the Seleucid kingdom was too weak and divided to threaten Judea, and the Hasmonean state expanded. Josephus says Hyrcanus also renewed the treaty with Rome (13.259–266).

Hyrcanus’s coins are the first well-dated Hasmonean coins, from about 130 BCE onward. They carry Hebrew inscriptions that name the high priest and “the Council (ḥever) of the Jews,” and the designs are plants and horns of plenty, never a human face. The Council may have been a body that represented the nation. The coins show a ruler who claimed priestly and national, not royal, status.

Josephus lists Hyrcanus’s conquests in a single sequence (Ant. 13.254–258). He took Medeba in Transjordan after a siege of six months and the nearby Samega. He took Shechem and Mount Gerizim, with “the nation of the Cutheans” (Samaritans), whose temple he says was “deserted two hundred years after it was built.” He took Adora and Marisa in Idumea, “and subdued all the Idumeans; and permitted them to stay in that country, if they would circumcise their genitals, and make use of the laws of the Jews” (Whiston’s translation). Josephus adds that, from then on, the Idumeans “were no other than Jews.” Later, Hyrcanus’s sons Aristobulus and Antigonus besieged Samaria, which Antiochus IX tried to relieve, and after a year took it and razed it (13.275–283). Scythopolis and the places near it also fell to the Jews (13.280–281).

The dates are less clear than the order of Josephus’s story. His sequence suggests that these events followed Antiochus VII’s death in 129 BCE, soon after. Excavations disagree. Yitzhak Magen’s excavations on Mount Gerizim date the destruction of the Samaritan temple to about 111–110 BCE, and the Idumean city of Maresha (Marisa) shows a destruction layer of about 112–111 BCE. Yonatan Adler gives about 112 BCE for the conquest of Idumea. Michał Marciak (2017) and Jonathan Bourgel (Journal of Biblical Literature 2016) have both reconsidered the evidence. In short, Josephus’s order of events points to the 120s BCE, and the archaeological evidence points to about 112–108 BCE [unconfirmed]. This lesson gives the range and does not choose between them.

What did “conversion” mean? Josephus says that the Idumeans were compelled to be circumcised and follow Jewish law, and says the same of the Itureans under Aristobulus I (Ant. 13.318–319, citing Timagenes). A century later, Herod’s father Antipater is called an Idumean (Ant. 14.8). Shaye Cohen (The Beginnings of Jewishness, 1999, ch. 4) argues that the Hasmonean policy was primarily political. The Idumeans were absorbed into the Judean ethnos and polity as citizens, and circumcision and the law were the markers of that membership, not an inner religious change. Others, among them Josephus’s own readers, took it as forced conversion. Josephus also reports that, under Jannaeus, a city that refused to change its “religious rites” for those of the Jews was destroyed (Ant. 13.397). The question matters for section 10.

At home, Hyrcanus broke with the Pharisees. Josephus tells how at a banquet a Pharisee named Eleazar told Hyrcanus to give up the high priesthood because his mother had been a captive. A Sadducee friend, Jonathan, persuaded the king that the Pharisees agreed with Eleazar, and Hyrcanus joined the Sadducees and abolished the Pharisees’ regulations (Ant. 13.288–298). Josephus explains that the Pharisees followed “a great many observances by succession from their fathers, which are not written in the laws of Moses,” and the Sadducees rejected them (13.297). The later Talmudic version of the quarrel (b. Qiddushin 66a) puts it under Alexander Jannaeus and not under Hyrcanus [unconfirmed]. Josephus also writes that Hyrcanus had “three of the greatest privileges”: rule of the nation, the high priesthood and the gift of prophecy (13.299–300). When he died in 104 BCE, Josephus says, he had left the government to his wife (13.302).

Why it matters

Hyrcanus made Judea a regional power and made its law the law of the conquered districts. Hasmonean rule now meant that some conquered peoples had to accept Judean customs, or leave. The Idumeans were absorbed into the Judean polity, and in the end a family of Idumean origin, the Herodians, took over the Hasmonean state.

6. Aristobulus I and Alexander Jannaeus, 104–76 BCE

Key dates
  1. 104–103Aristobulus I: first diadem; conquers Iturea
  2. 103–102Jannaeus king; war with Ptolemy IX
  3. c. 96Gaza destroyed
  4. c. 93Defeat at the Golan; revolt of the people
  5. c. 88Civil war; 800 crucified
  6. c. 83–80Greatest extent of the kingdom
  7. 76Jannaeus dies at Ragaba

Aristobulus I ruled for one year (104–103 BCE). Josephus says that he was the first to put on a diadem, and so changed the government into a kingdom (Ant. 13.301), but Strabo (16.2.40) gives that honour to Jannaeus. The coins of Aristobulus I are disputed [unconfirmed], so the sources for his title do not agree. Josephus says Aristobulus imprisoned his brothers and his mother. The mother, he says, starved to death in prison, and Aristobulus later had his favourite brother Antigonus killed (13.302–313). He then conquered much of Iturea in the north and made the people circumcise, citing Timagenes, who calls him “a man of candor” (13.318–319). He died soon after, of an illness which Josephus ties to remorse.

Alexander Jannaeus (Hebrew Yehonatan, 103–76 BCE) came to the throne because Aristobulus’s widow, Salome Alexandra, freed Aristobulus’s imprisoned brothers and made Alexander, whom Josephus calls the elder and more moderate, king. Josephus says he later killed one brother who wanted the throne (Ant. 13.320–323). Many later summaries say that she married him, but that is not in Josephus’s text as translated by Whiston [unconfirmed]. Jannaeus was an aggressive king, the most successful conqueror of the family, and a bad politician. In 103–102 BCE he attacked Ptolemais on the coast, which brought Ptolemy IX Lathyrus from Cyprus and, behind him, his mother Cleopatra III of Egypt. A hard battle by the Jordan went against Jannaeus (13.324–337), and Cleopatra’s Jewish general Ananias, according to Josephus, talked her out of annexing Judea (13.348–355). He then took Gaza after a long siege in about 96 BCE, and the coastal cities, then Gadara and Amathus in the east. About 93 BCE the Nabataean king Obodas ambushed him in the Golan and destroyed his army (13.371–375).

Defeat at home followed. At the Feast of Booths, as Jannaeus stood by the altar as high priest, the crowd pelted him with citrons and called him the son of a captive, unfit to sacrifice. He had six thousand of them killed and built a wooden barrier around the altar (Ant. 13.372–373). Josephus says the civil war lasted six years and cost fifty thousand Jewish lives (13.376). When Jannaeus’s opponents called in the Seleucid king Demetrius III Eukairos, Jannaeus lost a battle at Shechem. Then, in the end, many of Demetrius’s Jewish allies turned on him, and Jannaeus won. After capturing the town of Bethome, he took his prisoners to Jerusalem. “As he was feasting with his concubines, in the sight of all the city, he ordered about eight hundred of them to be crucified; and while they were living, he ordered the throats of their children and wives to be cut before their eyes” (13.380, Whiston). Josephus also tells the story in War 1.97. The Jews, he says, called the king “Thracian” for his cruelty. Pesher Nahum from Qumran (4Q169) speaks of a “Lion of Wrath” who “hangs men alive” and of a Demetrius who tried to enter Jerusalem on the advice of the “Seekers-after-Smooth-Things.” Many scholars read that as a Jannaeus-era memory of the crucifixions. The text names no king, so the link is an inference.

In his last years, Jannaeus won back his strongest position, in 83–80 BCE. Josephus lists his holdings (Ant. 13.395–397) along the coast from Mount Carmel to Rhinocolura, in the Galilee and the Golan, and in Moab and Gilead across the Jordan. This is the largest area the Hasmoneans ever held, and the map shows an approximation of it. He built or held desert fortresses, Alexandrium, Hyrcania, Machaerus and Masada; who first fortified which is uncertain [unconfirmed]. Josephus says Machaerus was first built by “Alexander the king of the Jews” (War 7.171). He died in 76 BCE during a siege at Ragaba east of the Jordan, after three years of a fever, having reigned twenty-seven years (13.398–406). On his deathbed, Josephus reports, he told his wife to hide his death until the fortress fell, to give some power to the Pharisees, and so to win the people to her (13.399–404).

Why it matters

Jannaeus’s reign shows both sides of Hasmonean rule: a kingdom at its greatest extent was run by a king whom many of his own people hated enough to rebel against. The ambivalence of Josephus, who condemns the crucifixions but admires the conquests, and the anger in the Qumran texts are why the Hasmoneans are remembered so unevenly.

7. Salome Alexandra and the brothers’ war, 76–63 BCE

Key dates
  1. 76–67Salome Alexandra rules; Hyrcanus II high priest
  2. 67Alexandra dies; Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II fight
  3. 65Aretas III besieges Jerusalem; Scaurus intervenes
  4. 64–63Both brothers appeal to Pompey at Damascus

Jannaeus left the kingdom to his wife Salome Alexandra (Hebrew Shelamzion), who ruled for nine years, 76–67 BCE. A woman could not be high priest, so she made the elder son, Hyrcanus II, high priest and kept royal power herself. Josephus’s verdict is favourable. He says that she kept the peace by giving real power to the Pharisees, the group Jannaeus had fought (Ant. 13.405–409; War 1.107–114). The Pharisees, he says, recalled exiles and then took revenge on their enemies, among them a man who had advised the crucifixions (War 1.111–114). The queen kept a large mercenary army, and Josephus says she bought off the Armenian king Tigranes when he approached Judea (Ant. 13.419–421). Her younger son Aristobulus II was the army’s favourite and spent these years gathering fortresses.

Hasmonean kings also built for themselves. Jericho was their winter capital, with a palace complex, baths and pools, described by Ehud Netzer (Hasmonean and Herodian Palaces at Jericho, 2001). The complex made lavish use of water, and it included ritual baths, which is one reason it features in the debate in section 10.

When Alexandra died in 67 BCE, the brothers went to war. Aristobulus II took fortresses and then marched on Jerusalem. Hyrcanus II met him near Jericho, was beaten when many of his troops deserted, and agreed to give up both titles and live as a private person (Ant. 14.4–7). That settlement lasted only a few years. Antipater, the Idumean son of Antipas, whom Jannaeus had made governor of Idumea, saw his chance. He persuaded Hyrcanus that Aristobulus meant to kill him and talked him into fleeing to the Nabataean king Aretas III at Petra, in return for twelve towns that Jannaeus had taken from the Nabataeans (14.8–18). Aretas and Hyrcanus besieged Aristobulus in the Temple in 65 BCE. During the siege the people asked a famous holy man, Onias “the circle-drawer,” to curse Aristobulus’s side. Josephus says he prayed that neither side would succeed, and that the besiegers stoned him (14.22–24). The Roman legate Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, sent by Pompey to Syria, then ordered Aretas to leave, after both brothers had offered him money, and he took Aristobulus’s side (14.29–33).

Why it matters

The civil war was a Hasmonean conflict, and Rome stepped in only because the brothers asked it to. Once Pompey was asked to judge between them, Rome could decide the government of Judea. The family that had won independence from one empire by playing empires against each other lost it in the same way.

8. Pompey, Antipater, the Parthians and Herod, 63–37 BCE

Key dates
  1. 63Pompey takes Jerusalem and enters the Temple
  2. 47Caesar rewards Antipater; Herod governs Galilee
  3. 43Antipater poisoned
  4. 40Parthians install Antigonus; Herod named king in Rome
  5. 37Herod takes Jerusalem; Antigonus executed

In 64–63 BCE Pompey was in Damascus, reorganizing the East after defeating Mithridates and Tigranes. Three delegations came to him there: Hyrcanus II, Aristobulus II, and a third group, “the nation.” Josephus says the third told Pompey that they did not want a king at all, since their fathers’ constitution was “to be subject to the priests of God” (Ant. 14.41). Diodorus (40.2) gives a similar report. Pompey postponed his decision. Aristobulus II then tried to resist, gave up the fortress of Alexandrium, and retreated to Jerusalem. The city split. Hyrcanus’s party opened the gates and Aristobulus’s men held the Temple Mount. Pompey besieged it for about three months. According to Josephus, it fell “on the day of the fast,” and about twelve thousand Jews were killed (Ant. 14.54–68). The exact date of the capture and the identity of the fast day are debated; Cassius Dio (37.16) says the Jews did not fight on the Sabbath. Pompey and his staff entered the Holy of Holies, but, Josephus reports, touched nothing in it (14.71–72).

Pompey’s settlement ended Hasmonean independence. Hyrcanus II was restored as high priest, without the title of king, and had to pay tribute (14.73–76). The coastal cities, Samaria, Scythopolis, Gadara and others were taken away and put under Rome’s province of Syria. Aristobulus II and his family were taken to Rome. Psalms of Solomon 2 is usually read as a Jewish response to Pompey’s capture, and Psalms of Solomon 17 is usually read as a criticism of the non-Davidic Hasmonean kings and a prayer for a Son of David [unconfirmed].

For twenty years Hyrcanus II was the nominal ruler, and Antipater was the real one. When Caesar was in difficulty in Alexandria in 48–47 BCE, Antipater brought Jewish troops to his aid. In return Caesar confirmed Hyrcanus as ethnarch, gave Antipater Roman citizenship and made him epitropos (procurator) of Judea, and allowed Jerusalem’s walls to be rebuilt (Ant. 14.127–144, 191, 199–200). Antipater put his son Phasael in charge of Jerusalem and his son Herod, a young man (Josephus’s manuscripts give his age as 15 in Antiquities and 25 in War [unconfirmed]), in charge of Galilee. Herod executed a bandit chief called Hezekiah and his men and was called to answer for it before the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem (14.158–184). Antipater was poisoned in 43 BCE by a rival, Malichus (14.289–293).

In 40 BCE the Parthians invaded Syria and Judea, led by the prince Pacorus and the satrap Barzapharnes. They installed the last Hasmonean ruler, Antigonus, the son of Aristobulus II, who had promised them a thousand talents and five hundred women (Ant. 14.330–333). Josephus reports that Hyrcanus’s ears were cut off, or that Antigonus bit them off, so that a mutilated man could never again serve as high priest (14.366). Phasael was captured and killed himself in prison (14.367–369). Antigonus issued coins as “Mattathias the high priest” in Hebrew and “King Antigonus” in Greek, with the Temple’s table and menorah on some of them (Meshorer). Herod fled, first to Masada, then to Petra, Alexandria and Rome. At Rome in 40 BCE (some scholars say 39 [unconfirmed]) Antony and Octavian had the Senate name him king of Judea (14.381–385).

It took Herod three years to take his kingdom. He returned in 39 BCE with Roman help, took Galilee and Jericho, and in 37 BCE besieged Jerusalem with the Roman general Sosius. Before the siege, at Samaria, Herod married the Hasmonean princess Mariamne, granddaughter of both Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II (Ant. 14.465–467). Josephus says that the siege lasted about five months. The city fell in the summer of 37 BCE; Josephus dates it by the consuls Agrippa and Gallus, and many historians still debate 37 against 36 [unconfirmed]. The Roman troops plundered, and Herod paid them to stop. Antigonus gave himself up to Sosius and was taken to Antony. Strabo, quoted by Josephus (Ant. 15.8–10), says Antony had him beheaded at Antioch. Cassius Dio (49.22) says he was flogged and then killed. With his death, Josephus notes, a government that had lasted 126 years ended (14.490).

Herod’s rule was long, and it was a continued struggle with the Hasmonean legacy. He had Hyrcanus II, then an old man, executed in about 30 BCE [unconfirmed]. He made Mariamne’s brother Aristobulus III high priest in 35 BCE and had him drowned in a pool at Jericho the same year (Ant. 15.50–56). He executed Mariamne herself about 29 BCE [unconfirmed] (15.222–236), and her mother Alexandra soon after [unconfirmed]. Later, he executed two of his own sons by Mariamne, Alexander and Aristobulus. Mariamne’s sons were killed, but through them Hasmonean descent passed to later Herodians, among them Herod Agrippa I, her grandson. The Herodian kings and Roman procurators ruled Judea until the Great Revolt of 66 CE.

Why it matters

The Hasmonean state fell because of a civil war and an appeal to Rome. Pompey ended its independence, Antipater’s family used Rome to rule, and Herod ended the dynasty by conquest, marriage and murder. For Jewish history this makes 63 BCE, not 37, the real turning point: Judea was a Roman dependency from then on.

9. Society, religion and the state

Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes. Josephus first mentions “three sects among the Jews” in the time of Jonathan (Ant. 13.171). The Pharisees, he says, passed on observances “from their fathers” that were not in the written laws of Moses, and had the multitude on their side. The Sadducees, who had the confidence of the rich, rejected anything not in the written word. The Essenes, whom he describes at length elsewhere, lived a communal life (Ant. 13.171–173; War 2.119–166). Pliny the Elder (Natural History 5.73) places an Essene community above the western shore of the Dead Sea. Josephus’s descriptions were written for Greek and Roman readers, long after the period, and modern scholars disagree about how far they can be trusted. What is clear is that the Hasmonean kings stood in the middle of the conflict, with Hyrcanus I breaking with the Pharisees, Jannaeus fighting them, and Alexandra giving them power.

Qumran and the Scrolls. The Dead Sea Scrolls, found from 1947 onward in caves near Qumran, include biblical manuscripts, such as the great Isaiah scroll, and sectarian texts. Many scholars identify the community that kept the sectarian texts with the Essenes, though this identification is challenged. The commentaries (pesharim) read prophecy as a code for the group’s own time, and they mention a “Teacher of Righteousness,” a “Wicked Priest” and a “Lion of Wrath” without naming any of them. Scholars have proposed Jonathan or Simon as the Wicked Priest, and Jannaeus has some supporters [unconfirmed]. Pesher Habakkuk’s “Kittim” are Romans, so that text was written after 63 BCE. The date at which the Qumran settlement was founded is disputed, with some placing it in the late second or early first century BCE [unconfirmed]. The Scrolls show a group for whom the Hasmonean high priesthood was illegitimate, and so a Jewish view of Hasmonean rule that Josephus does not give.

Coins and images. The Hasmoneans minted their own coins from about 130 BCE. Hyrcanus I’s coins are Hebrew-only and carry no human figure. Later kings, Jannaeus especially, added Greek, and some of his coins are bilingual, though they too avoid the human face. Common symbols on the coins are the cornucopia, the anchor, the star and the lily. Antigonus’s last coins show the Temple table and menorah. The avoidance of images is one of the pieces of evidence discussed by Yonatan Adler (section 10).

Rome. 1 Maccabees 8 says that Judah, after hearing of Rome’s defeats of Macedon and the Seleucids, sent Eupolemus and Jason to Rome, and that the Senate agreed to a treaty of mutual aid. The text of the treaty, in 8:23–32, is given in Greek translation, and Jonathan and Simon renewed it (12:1–4; 14:16–24; 15:15–24). The same book also records letters to the Spartans, who are said to share a kinship with the Jews through Abraham (12:5–23). Historians accept that some agreement was made with Rome, but the dating, the exact terms and the authenticity of the documents are debated. Whatever its legal form, the agreement was a diplomatic resource. Letters preserved in 1 Macc 15:15–24 and in Josephus (Ant. 13.259–266) show Rome asking kings not to harm the Jews, and in the end Rome became the arbiter of the Hasmonean quarrels.

Hellenization. The family that fought Antiochus IV’s Hellenizing decrees quickly adopted Hellenistic habits. The kings took Greek names: Alexander, Aristobulus, Antigonus. They hired foreign mercenaries and built Hellenistic palaces. They put Greek on coins, sent embassies in the Greek style, and made treaties with Hellenistic states. Lawrence Schiffman describes the dynasty as increasingly Hellenized. Erich Gruen argues that Jewish and Hellenistic culture were not opposed in the first place; Jews, he says, expressed themselves in Hellenistic forms as part of how they asserted a Jewish identity (Heritage and Hellenism, 1998). So the question is how to describe the mix, and historians differ.

Priest-kings. Mattathias’s family came from the priestly course of Joarib (1 Macc 2:1), not from the high-priestly line of Zadok, and they were not descended from David. The assembly of 140 BCE made Simon leader and high priest “until a trustworthy prophet should arise” (1 Macc 14:41), which is an admission that his position was provisional. His descendants later took the title of king. Qumran texts, the Psalms of Solomon and, in Josephus, the objection of Eleazar to Hyrcanus, show that contemporaries questioned the family’s right. The citron incident and the delegation to Pompey in 63 BCE show the same doubt. Combining priest and king, in a nation whose Scripture assigns these to different lines, was a choice with long consequences.

Why it matters

The Hasmonean period is where the Jewish groups we know from the first century CE, the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes, are first seen in the sources. The evidence for them is thin and mostly from later writers. Hasmonean politics gave their quarrels a stake in who ruled and in how the law was to be applied.

10. A scholarly debate: Yonatan Adler on the origins of Judaism

The Hasmonean period is central to a recent argument about when ordinary Judeans began to keep the Torah as law. Yonatan Adler, an archaeologist at Ariel University, set out the argument in The Origins of Judaism: An Archaeological-Historical Reappraisal (Yale University Press, 2022). This section reports his claims and the main responses. It does not choose between them, and every claim below is attributed to the scholar who makes it. The lesson’s other sections do not depend on the book.

The question and the method. Adler says that his subject is social history, not the history of ideas or of the composition of the Bible. He asks when the Torah’s laws became practised, widely, as binding law among Judeans, and not when it was written. He says it is likely that the Torah existed for centuries before it was widely known. His method, as he describes it, is to start from the first century CE, when the sources show practices that are clearly observed, and move backward through the evidence to find its earliest traces. That gives him a latest possible date for the change, a terminus ante quem. He treats the lack of evidence for earlier periods as meaningful but concedes that the absence of evidence may reflect only what has survived.

The first-century baseline. In an article on TheTorah.com, Adler lists what the first century CE shows. Philo, Josephus and Roman authors say that Jews abstain from pork. Hundreds of stepped immersion pools (miqva’ot) and chalk vessels have been found. Art avoids human and animal figures. Judean Desert caves have dozens of tefillin and a few possible mezuzot. Sabbath, Passover, Yom Kippur and Sukkot are all attested.

The earliest evidence, by Adler’s reading. Going backward, Adler reports that he finds the evidence thins out around the middle of the second century BCE. In his account, immersion pools and chalk vessels appear about the end of the second century BCE. The earliest tefillin from Qumran date, he says, to the late second or early first century BCE. Hasmonean coins appear about 130 BCE, and the earliest well-dated ones, under Hyrcanus I, avoid figures; the name, the title and the phrase “the assembly of the Judeans” make a kind of textual portrait. He also points to Roman decrees protecting Jewish Sabbath observance (Ant. 14.226 ff.; 16.163, 168) and to Cicero’s remark about pork around 70 BCE (Plutarch, Cicero 7.6). In an interview in the Times of Israel (5 April 2023) he says no text from before the middle of the second century BCE speaks of Judeans abstaining from pork. He adds that a lack of pig bones at a site does not by itself show a taboo, since pig bones depend on economic and ecological circumstances.

The Persian and early Hellenistic periods. Adler cites evidence that, he says, does not fit a Torah-observing population in earlier centuries. Catfish remains found in Persian-period Jerusalem (Adler and Lernau, Tel Aviv 48, 2021) are, in his view, hard to square with the food laws. Coins minted in Judea in the fourth and early third centuries carry figural images, such as the Athenian owl, and names such as “Yehizqiyah the governor” and “Yohanan the priest.” The Jewish military colony at Elephantine in Egypt, whose papyri he reads as showing a reverence for other deities, never mentions the days of the week. Adler argues that the “Passover Papyrus” of 419 BCE is mostly reconstructed, and that the Passover content falls in the reconstructed parts; he calls the argument that it shows Torah observance circular. He treats Ezra and Nehemiah as stories, not histories, and notes that Nehemiah 13 itself reports Sabbath-breaking and intermarriage soon after the public reading of the Torah.

Candidate explanations. Adler proposes two candidate periods for the change. One is the Ptolemaic court in about 275 BCE, a suggestion he links to Michael LeFebvre. The other is the Hasmonean adoption of the Pentateuch as the law of the land, which he compares to a combination of the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution; he cites Reinhard Kratz (2015) and John Collins (2017) as scholars with related views. On the persecution under Antiochus IV, he suggests that it targeted the Temple cult and culture, and that the framing in terms of the Torah was added later by 1 and 2 Maccabees.

The Hasmonean link. If the Hasmoneans made the Torah a law of the land, the evidence for them enforcing it matters. Adler cites Josephus’s statement that Hyrcanus allowed the Idumeans to remain if they were circumcised and used the laws of the Jews (Ant. 13.257–258), and that Aristobulus I did the same to the Itureans (13.318–319). He also points to Josephus’s report that Jannaeus destroyed a city whose people would not adopt Jewish customs (13.397). Josephus’s account of the Pharisees’ “ancestral laws” that are not in the laws of Moses and are rejected by the Sadducees (13.297) is part of the same picture of law as contested politics. Adler says that Judah, Jonathan or Simon “perhaps” also enforced the laws on Judeans, but “we don’t have evidence for this.” Shaye Cohen’s reading of the Idumean episode, as primarily a political incorporation, is one alternative to a purely religious reading.

Responses and critiques.

  • Malka Simkovich (Jewish Review of Books, Winter 2024) argues that Adler dismisses pre-Hasmonean texts such as Tobit 1:10–13, that the archaeology covers only sites in Israel and says little about the diaspora, and that practice and ideas are hard to separate, since many laws were “unwritten” (she cites Philo). She also asks why a shift after the exile is not a better fit, and she is wary of reasoning from absence.
  • Adler’s reply (JRB, 24 May 2024) says that the book avoids questions of belief and asks when ordinary Jews began to treat the Torah as binding law. He presents it as a correction to the habit of giving the ideas of literate elites priority over the practices of ordinary Jews. Simkovich’s rejoinder is that data from particular sites should not outweigh texts.
  • Benjamin D. Gordon (AJS Review 49, 2024) calls the book essential reading and sees it as extending E. P. Sanders’s “common Judaism.” He suggests reading it alongside Andrea Berlin’s work, and warns that Judea was sparsely populated, so that the survival of evidence may limit the argument.
  • Joseph Scales (Reading Religion, 28 July 2023) thinks the question may not be settled with the material now available (“interpretations are not themselves data”). He notes that immersion pools are common in Jerusalem but rare elsewhere, with only four excavated at Gamla (c. 100 BCE–68 CE). He doubts treating 1 and 2 Maccabees as evidence of practice while rejecting earlier texts. He agrees that the Hasmoneans used Torah observance in their expression of power, and reports Adler’s suggestion that Torah observance offered “a viable and attractive alternative to Hellenism.”

The debate has several moving parts: which texts count as evidence of practice, whether archaeology of a few sites can stand for a population, and whether the absence of early evidence is meaningful. How widely the field accepts Adler’s thesis is not something this lesson can measure; the responses above are a sample and not a survey. For the Hasmonean story, the relevant point is a narrower one: Hasmonean rule was a time when Torah law and political power were closely joined, and scholars disagree about how new this was.

Why it matters

Whether the Hasmoneans introduced Torah observance, enforced it, or inherited it, they are the first Judean rulers whose actions the sources describe in terms of the Torah’s laws. Adler’s book is the most recent systematic challenge to the assumption that this was an old practice, and the replies to it show how much depends on what counts as evidence.

11. Legacy and Hanukkah

Hanukkah (“dedication”) is the main living memory of the Hasmoneans. The earliest sources do not describe the holiday as we know it. 2 Maccabees (10:1–8) says that Judah and his companions, after cleansing the Temple, kept eight days of rejoicing “after the manner of Booths,” with lamps lit, and decided that the whole nation should observe the days every year. Josephus calls the festival “Lights,” and does not explain why (Ant. 12.325). 2 Maccabees opens with two letters, and the first, dated to 188 of the Seleucid era (124 BCE), invites the Jews of Egypt to keep the feast (2 Macc 1:9); its authenticity is debated. 1 Maccabees gives the date, the 25th of Chislev, and the eight days (4:52–59). A calendar of festivals called Megillat Taanit lists the 25th of Kislev as a day on which fasting is forbidden. The Mishnah mentions Hanukkah only in passing (m. Ta’anit 2:10; m. Bava Kamma 6:6; m. Megillah 3:6).

The story of a single jar of oil that burned for eight days first appears in the Babylonian Talmud (b. Shabbat 21b), centuries after the events. Vered Noam (Hebrew Union College Annual 73, 2002) argues that it was a late, literary development, in which the earlier Hebrew scholion to Megillat Taanit has no oil story and another version mentions oil without a miracle [unconfirmed]. The Talmudic details here come from secondary summaries and should be checked against the Talmud itself. Many historians suggest that the rabbis, who lived under Rome and did not favour armed revolt, gave the holiday a spiritual meaning, and Hasmonean kingship, held by a non-Davidic dynasty, may also have been unwelcome to them [unconfirmed]. Some link the haftarah of Zechariah 4 (“not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit”) with the same trend [unconfirmed].

The books of Maccabees were not included in the Hebrew Bible. They were preserved by Greek-speaking Christians; 1 and 2 Maccabees are part of the Catholic and Orthodox canons, and the Maccabean martyrs are honoured in Christian tradition. Josephus kept much of the Hasmonean story, and the Scrolls preserve a sectarian view of it. In modern times, the Maccabees became a symbol for Zionism: the Maccabi sports clubs and the first Maccabiah games, held in 1932, took their name. Hanukkah itself has been read as a story of religious freedom, of national liberation, and also, in some modern retellings, as a story of civil war among Jews. The sources support each of these readings only in part.

For further reading, see the bibliography. The primary sources are 1 and 2 Maccabees and Josephus, and the best single modern histories are Atkinson, Grabbe and Schiffman, with Bar-Kochva for Judah’s campaigns and Gruen and Cohen for Hellenism and identity.

Why it matters

The Hasmonean kingdom was the last sovereign Jewish state in the land before modern Israel, apart from the short-lived Bar Kokhba state of 132–135 CE, yet the rabbinic tradition remembered them selectively, and the best evidence for them came from Josephus and the Books of Maccabees. Knowing who wrote each source and when is the way to tell the history from the later commemoration.

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1What did Antiochus IV’s decrees ban, and what are the three main explanations modern historians give for them?
Answer. According to 1 Macc 1:41–64 and 2 Macc 6:1–11 they banned Temple sacrifice, Sabbath rest, circumcision and possession of the law, and they set up a pagan altar in the Temple in December 167 BCE. Bickerman blamed radical Hellenizing Jews, Tcherikover blamed a response to a Jewish revolt, and Gruen rejects both and sees a display of royal power after the humiliation in Egypt.
2Why did Mattathias and his followers decide to fight on the Sabbath?
Answer. After a thousand Jews, according to 1 Macc 2:29–41, let themselves be killed rather than fight on the day of rest, Mattathias’s group ruled that they might fight in self-defence (Josephus repeats this at Ant. 12.272–277).
3What happened in 164 BCE, and what do the earliest sources say about it?
Answer. Judah cleansed the Temple and rededicated the altar on 25 Chislev. 1 Macc 4:36–59 and 2 Macc 10:1–8 describe an eight-day festival like Booths; Josephus calls it “Lights.” The oil miracle is not in these sources and first appears in the Babylonian Talmud.
4Name the five sons of Mattathias and say which of them became the rulers of Judea.
Answer. John Gaddi, Simon Thassi, Judah Maccabee, Eleazar Avaran and Jonathan Apphus. Judah led from 166 to 160, Jonathan was high priest from 152 to 143, and Simon ruled from 142 to 134. Only Simon’s line continued the dynasty.
5What changed in 142–140 BCE?
Answer. The “yoke of the nations” was removed in 142 when the Seleucid king Demetrius II released the Jews from tribute, and documents were dated by Simon’s years. The Akra was taken in 141. In 140 an assembly confirmed Simon as leader and high priest, “until a trustworthy prophet should arise” (1 Macc 14:41).
6What does Josephus say Hyrcanus I did in Idumea, and how do scholars read it?
Answer. Josephus says that Hyrcanus took Adora and Marisa and allowed the Idumeans to stay only if they were circumcised and used the laws of the Jews (Ant. 13.257–258). Some read this as forced religious conversion; Shaye Cohen reads it as political incorporation into the Judean ethnos. The dating (Josephus’s order versus the archaeology of about 112 BCE) is also debated.
7Why is Alexander Jannaeus remembered so ambivalently?
Answer. He was the great conqueror of the dynasty, with the kingdom at its greatest extent, but his own people rebelled, and, according to Josephus, he crucified about 800 opponents and killed their families (Ant. 13.380). Pesher Nahum’s “Lion of Wrath” who “hangs men alive” is often linked to him, though the text names no king.
8How did the Hasmonean state lose its independence, and what role did Rome play?
Answer. After Alexandra’s death in 67 BCE the sons Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II fought a civil war, and each appealed to Pompey. Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BCE, entered the Temple, ended the monarchy and made Hyrcanus a high priest under Roman supervision. Antipater and his son Herod rose in this system and, after the Parthian invasion of 40 BCE, Herod took Jerusalem in 37 BCE.
9What is Yonatan Adler’s main claim in The Origins of Judaism (2022), and what kind of evidence does he use?
Answer. He argues that the evidence for Judeans widely observing the Torah as binding law goes back only to about the middle of the second century BCE, and that the Hasmoneans may have made it the law of the land. He works backwards from first-century CE evidence (immersion pools, abstention from pork, aniconism, Sabbath, tefillin and mezuzot) and reads earlier material, such as Elephantine and Persian-period finds, as showing the opposite.
10Name two critiques of Adler’s argument, and say how he responded to one of them.
Answer. Simkovich argues that he dismisses pre-Hasmonean texts such as Tobit, relies on sites in Israel, and reasons from absence. Scales doubts that the question can be settled and notes that few miqva’ot are known outside Jerusalem. Gordon warns that Judea’s sparse population limits what survives. In reply to Simkovich, Adler says the book is about when ordinary people began to treat the Torah as binding law, and that he is correcting the preference for literati’s ideas over ordinary practice.

40 BCEParthian invasion; Antigonus installed; Hyrcanus mutilated; Herod named king in Rome
37 BCEHerod and Sosius take Jerusalem; Antigonus executed (some say 36)
c. 35 BCEAristobulus III made high priest and drowned
c. 30 BCEHyrcanus II executed by Herod
c. 29 BCEMariamne executed
4 BCEHerod dies

Bibliography

Editions are noted where I checked them. Entries without a link were identified from library or publisher records or from the works’ own citations, not from the books themselves; items marked unconfirmed need checking before they are cited.

Primary sources

  • 1 and 2 Maccabees. The main narrative sources; 1 Maccabees favours the Hasmoneans, 2 Maccabees covers 175–161 BCE in an epitome of Jason of Cyrene. The Greek text of 1 Maccabees may rest on a Hebrew original. In the Septuagint and the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.
  • Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 12–16 and Jewish War 1 (Loeb Classical Library). Antiquities 12–14 is in Loeb no. 365 (1933). The quotations in this lesson are from Whiston’s translation, which is old and sometimes unreliable.
  • Polybius, Diodorus Siculus, Strabo (Loeb Classical Library). Short passages on Antiochus IV’s Egyptian campaigns, on Antiochus VII and Jerusalem, and on Hasmonean Judea (Strabo 16.2.40).
  • Megillat Taanit. An Aramaic list of festival days with later scholia, which includes 25 Kislev.
  • Geza Vermes, The Complete Dead Sea Scrolls in English (London: Penguin). Translations of the Scrolls, including Pesher Habakkuk and Pesher Nahum.

Modern histories

  • Kenneth Atkinson, A History of the Hasmonean State: Josephus and Beyond (London: Bloomsbury T&T Clark, 2016). The most recent full account of the dynasty.
  • Lester L. Grabbe, A History of the Jews and Judaism in the Second Temple Period, vol. 3: The Maccabaean Revolt, Hasmonaean Rule, and Herod the Great (175–4 BCE) (London: T&T Clark, 2020), and Judaism from Cyrus to Hadrian (Minneapolis: Fortress, 1992).
  • Bezalel Bar-Kochva, Judas Maccabaeus: The Jewish Struggle against the Seleucids (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989). The military history of Judah’s campaigns.
  • Daniel R. Schwartz, 2 Maccabees, Commentaries on Early Jewish Literature (Berlin: de Gruyter, 2008).
  • Seth Schwartz, Imperialism and Jewish Society, 200 B.C.E. to 640 C.E. (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2001).
  • Erich S. Gruen, Heritage and Hellenism: The Reinvention of Jewish Tradition (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1998); and “Hellenism and Persecution: Antiochus IV and the Jews,” in Hellenistic History and Culture, ed. P. Green (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1993), ch. 8.
  • Shaye J. D. Cohen, From the Maccabees to the Mishnah (Philadelphia: Westminster, 1987; 3rd ed., Louisville: Westminster John Knox, 2014); and The Beginnings of Jewishness (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1999), ch. 4 on the Idumeans.
  • Lawrence H. Schiffman, From Text to Tradition (Hoboken: Ktav, 1991), and his Hasmonean overview on the Center for Online Judaic Studies site.
  • Doron Mendels, The Rise and Fall of Jewish Nationalism (New York: Doubleday, 1992).
  • Uriel Rappaport, The House of the Hasmoneans (Hebrew; Jerusalem: Yad Ben-Zvi, 2013).
  • Tessa Rajak, Josephus: The Historian and His Society (London: Duckworth, 1983).
  • Jonathan A. Goldstein, I Maccabees (Anchor Bible 41, 1976) and II Maccabees (Anchor Bible 41A, 1983) (Garden City: Doubleday).
  • Joseph Sievers, The Hasmoneans and Their Supporters (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1990).
  • Elias Bickerman, Der Gott der Makkabäer (Berlin: Schocken, 1937); Victor Tcherikover, Hellenistic Civilization and the Jews (Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society, 1959). The classic explanations of Antiochus IV’s decrees.
  • The Cambridge History of Judaism, vol. 2, The Hellenistic Age, ed. W. D. Davies and L. Finkelstein (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989); vol. 3, The Early Roman Period, ed. W. Horbury, W. D. Davies and J. Sturdy (1999).

Archaeology, Idumea, Samaria

  • Ehud Netzer, Hasmonean and Herodian Palaces at Jericho (Jerusalem: Israel Exploration Society, 2001).
  • Ya’akov Meshorer, A Treasury of Jewish Coins (Nyack and Jerusalem: Amphora, 2001).
  • Jonathan Bourgel, “The Destruction of the Samaritan Temple by John Hyrcanus: A Reconsideration,” Journal of Biblical Literature 135, no. 3 (2016), from p. 505.
  • Michał Marciak, “Idumea and the Idumeans in Josephus’ Story of Hellenistic-Early Roman Palestine (Ant. XII–XX)” (2017). unconfirmed: dating and journal not checked
  • Yitzhak Magen on Mount Gerizim, in The New Encyclopedia of Archaeological Excavations in the Holy Land, s.v. “Gerizim, Mount.” unconfirmed: second-hand

Qumran, Hanukkah

  • Vered Noam, “The Miracle of the Cruse of Oil: The Metamorphosis of a Legend,” Hebrew Union College Annual 73 (2002): 191–226. unconfirmed: some listings give 2003

  • Adler, “When Did Jews Start Observing Torah?”, TheTorah.com. thetorah.com
  • Amanda Borschel-Dan, “What Matters Now to archaeologist Prof. Yonatan Adler: The origins of Judaism,” Times of Israel, 5 April 2023. timesofisrael.com
  • Malka Simkovich, “Origin Stories,” Jewish Review of Books, Winter 2024. jewishreviewofbooks.com
  • Adler, “A Torah Exchange: Yonatan Adler Responds to Malka Simkovich,” JRB, 24 May 2024, link; and Simkovich’s reply, link.
  • Benjamin D. Gordon, review in AJS Review 49 (2024), doi 10.1353/ajs.2024.a926065. unconfirmed: issue number and contents read only from a snippet

  • Adler and Lernau, Tel Aviv 48 (2021): 5–26 (the Persian-period fish remains), and Adler, “Purity, Pottery, and Judaean Ethnicity in the Hasmonean Period,” Journal of Ancient Judaism 12 (2021): 391–432.

Data and map sources

  • Basemap: Natural Earth (public domain), 1:50m land and countries, 1:10m lakes and rivers, drawn with the Albers map engine built for The House of Timur. Borders are today’s borders; none is an ancient border.
  • Places: modern-site coordinates. The ancient site of Modi’in is not identified, so the marker is the modern city’s area. Positions are approximate for antiquity.
  • Shaded areas: hand-drawn approximations of the territory the sources imply for each period. They are not surveyed borders and are meant to show the order of magnitude and direction of expansion.
  • Dates: the conventional chronology is used. Where sources or scholars differ (for example 37 or 36 BCE for the fall of Jerusalem, and the date of the conquest of Idumea), the text gives the range. Items that could not be checked against a source other than Wikipedia are marked [unconfirmed].
